title: Shell Scripting in zsh
sub: Variables, tests, loops, functions and options: turn one-liners into tools, and build netcheck.zsh
goals: Write an executable zsh script with a shebang, arguments, exit codes and a place on your PATH
Use variables, arrays, associative arrays and parameter expansion correctly under zsh's rules
Branch and loop with [[ ]], if, case, for, while and select, and read input line by line
Structure code with functions, local variables and getopts or zparseopts option parsing
Make scripts fail safely with setopt, trap and cleanup, and debug them with xtrace
Build netcheck.zsh, a coloured network health report that exits non-zero on failure

blocks.text: A script is a text file of commands that the shell runs in order, plus the few constructs that turn a list into a program: variables, decisions, loops and functions. If you can type a pipeline, you can already script; this chapter adds the structure that makes a pipeline reusable, safe and pleasant to run at three in the morning when something is broken. You will finish by building `netcheck.zsh`, a tool you will keep extending through the networking chapters, and a backup script with rotation.

Make a folder for scripts and stay in it while you read: `mkdir -p ~/lab/scripts && cd ~/lab/scripts`. Keep `~/lab` files around; the examples use `hosts.txt`, `ips.txt`, `users.csv` and `access.log` from there (`../hosts.txt` and so on). Editing: use PyCharm, or `nano`; the keys are in [Thinking like a programmer](#thinking).
From command to script

A **shebang** is a first line that begins with `#!` and names the interpreter. When you run a file directly, the kernel reads those two bytes, finds the path after them and runs that program with your file as its argument. No shebang, no idea which language the file is in: zsh then hands the file to `/bin/sh`, which on macOS is bash in POSIX mode and fails on zsh-only syntax.
A freshly created file is not executable. The permission bit has to be set, and because the current folder is not on `PATH`, you name the file with a path prefix:

blocks.code:
$ ./hello.zsh
zsh: permission denied: ./hello.zsh
$ chmod +x hello.zsh
$ ./hello.zsh
Hello from ./hello.zsh on macbook.local
$ zsh hello.zsh
Hello from hello.zsh on macbook.local

blocks.text: Three ways to run a script differ in important ways:

head: Command
What happens
Needs the execute bit
rows: kernel reads the shebang and starts a **new process** with that interpreter
you choose the interpreter, the shebang is just a comment
commands run **inside your current shell**, so variables, `cd` and functions persist afterwards

blocks.text: `PATH` lists directories searched for commands, and `.` is deliberately absent from it. If it were present, a file named `ls` dropped into a download folder would run instead of the real one the moment you typed `ls` there. The explicit `./` makes you say "this file, here, on purpose".

`#!/bin/zsh` is the system zsh and exists on every Mac. `#!/usr/bin/env zsh` finds the first `zsh` on your `PATH`, which would be a Homebrew build if you installed one. For scripts that only use macOS tools, `#!/bin/zsh` is predictable. Avoid `#!/bin/sh` for zsh code: on macOS `sh` runs bash in POSIX mode, which does not understand zsh-only syntax such as `${(U)v}`, 1-indexed arrays or glob qualifiers.
Putting scripts on your PATH
Create `~/bin`, put scripts there without the `.zsh` suffix if you like, and add the folder to `PATH` in `~/.zshrc`:

blocks.code:
mkdir -p ~/bin
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc
cp hello.zsh ~/bin/hello && chmod +x ~/bin/hello
hello

blocks.text: zsh remembers where it found each command in a hash table; after adding a new file to a `PATH` folder the shell may not see it until you run `rehash` (it usually notices on its own).
Variables and special parameters

A variable is a name bound to a string (or an array, below). **Assignment has no spaces around `=`.** `n=5` assigns; `n = 5` tries to run a command called `n` with arguments `=` and `5`. Read a variable with `$n` or the unambiguous `${n}` (needed in `${n}th`). Names are case sensitive and by convention lower case for your own variables, upper case for environment variables.

head: Command
Effect
rows: create or change a shell variable, visible in this shell and its functions only
also copy it into the environment of every program started afterwards
constant: any later assignment is an error
inside a function: variable that disappears when the function returns
set a variable for that one command only: `LC_ALL=C sort file`

blocks.text: The special parameters
The shell sets these for you. You will use them in every script:

head: Parameter
Holds
Notes
rows: name of the script as you invoked it
inside a function zsh sets it to the function name unless you `setopt NO_FUNCTION_ARGZERO`; store `${0:t}` at the top
all arguments, each as a separate word when written `"$@"`
use this to pass arguments on unchanged
all arguments joined into one string when written `"$*"`
exit status of the last command
reset by every command, so save it with `rc=$?` before using it twice
handy for unique temp names, `mktemp` is better
process ID of the last background job
last argument of the previous command

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
echo "script: $0"
echo "count:  $#"
echo "first:  $1"
echo "all:    $@"
for a in "$@"; do echo "  arg: [$a]"; done
ls /nonexistent 2>/dev/null
echo "last status: $?"

$ chmod +x args.zsh
$ ./args.zsh one "two words" three
script: ./args.zsh
count:  3
first:  one
all:    one two words three
  arg: [one]
  arg: [two words]
  arg: [three]
last status: 1

blocks.text: Notice that `"two words"` stayed one argument, and that `"$@"` kept it that way inside the loop. On macOS `ls` reports a missing file with status 1; GNU `ls` on Linux reports 2, which is the kind of detail to check rather than hard-code.
Quoting rules for scripts
In interactive use a quoting slip costs you a retry. In a script it can delete the wrong files. Habits that prevent most trouble:

items.text: **Double-quote every expansion that holds a value you did not write yourself**: `"$file"`, `"$(command)"`, `"$@"`. Filenames and user input contain spaces.
Single quotes pass text through untouched; use them for `awk` programs, `sed` scripts and regexes.

zsh does **not** split unquoted variables on whitespace (bash does), so `ls $file` with `file="my notes.txt"` passes one argument in zsh. That is a safer default, but do not rely on it if the script may be run with bash; quote anyway.

zsh **does** drop an unquoted variable that is empty: `printf '%s|%s\n' $empty x` passes only one argument. Quote it (`"$empty"`) when an empty value must still count as an argument. This is the classic reason a `printf` or `test` call behaves oddly with an empty variable.
To split a string on purpose use `${=var}` (split on whitespace) or `${(s:,:)var}` (split on commas).

tokens.exp: path to the script; the kernel reads its shebang line to pick the interpreter
becomes $1
quotes keep this as a single argument, becoming $2
becomes $3 and brings $# to 3

blocks.text: Arrays and associative arrays

An **array** is an ordered list of strings. In zsh, **indexes start at 1**, negative indexes count from the end, and `${#arr}` is the length. This differs from bash (which starts at 0), so be careful when copying snippets from the web.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
hosts=(pi nas printer)
echo $hosts[1] $hosts[-1] ${#hosts}      # first, last, length
hosts+=(router)                           # append
echo ${hosts[2,3]}                        # a slice
echo ${(j:, :)hosts}                      # join with ", "
typeset -A port                           # associative array: string keys
port=(ssh 22 http 80)
port[dns]=53
for k in ${(ko)port}; do printf '%-5s %s\n' $k $port[$k]; done
echo ${+port[ssh]} ${+port[ftp]}          # 1 if the key exists, else 0
echo ${#port}                             # number of keys

$ zsh arrays.zsh
pi printer 3
nas printer
pi, nas, printer, router
dns   53
http  80
ssh   22
1 0
3

blocks.text: `${(ko)port}` lists the keys sorted (`k` keys, `o` order). `${(kv)port}` yields alternating keys and values, and `${(v)port}` the values. Without `o` the order is unspecified, as in `awk`.

Two idioms turn command output into an array. `files=(*.log(N))` collects a glob (the `N` qualifier makes it empty instead of an error when nothing matches). `lines=("${(@f)$(cmd)}")` splits the command's output on newlines, one element per line, preserving blanks and spaces inside lines.

tokens.exp: keyword: repeat while the next command succeeds
set the field separator to a comma for this one read
read a line, treating backslashes literally
variables that receive the four fields; the last would take any remainder
end of the condition, start of the loop body
body: print only developers
end of the loop
feed the loop from a command whose output skips the header line

blocks.name: typeset
blocks.sum: Declare variables with attributes: array, associative array, integer, float, read-only, local.

how.text: `typeset` (also spelled `declare` in zsh) creates a variable and attaches attributes to it. Inside a function it makes the variable local. `-A` creates an associative array (a map from string keys to values), `-a` an indexed array, `-i` an integer (assignments are evaluated arithmetically), `-F n` a floating-point number printed with n decimals, `-r` read-only and `-x` exported.
Plain `name=(a b c)` already makes an array, so `typeset -a` is mostly documentation. `-A` is required for maps, because `name=(k v k v)` alone would build an indexed array of four elements.

flags.d: Float printed with n decimal places: `typeset -F 2 r; (( r = 22 / 7.0 ))` gives `3.14`.
Read-only; any later assignment fails with "read-only variable".

examples.desc: Count requests per status code in a map
examples.code:
typeset -A seen
awk '{print $9}' access.log | while read -r code; do (( seen[$code]++ )); done
for k in ${(ko)seen}; do print "$k $seen[$k]"; done

examples.desc: A constant that cannot be changed by accident
Load key and value pairs from a command into a map
examples.code: typeset -A role; role=($(tail -n +2 users.csv | awk -F, '{print $1, $2}')); print ${role[alice]}

gotchas: A pipeline's last stage may run in a subshell in other shells, so a loop that updates a variable can lose its changes. zsh runs the last stage of a pipeline in the **current** shell, which is why the first example works here but not in bash.

blocks.text: Parameter expansion

Parameter expansion is the shell's built-in string toolkit: defaults, trimming, replacing and case changes, with no subprocess. It replaces many `sed`, `cut` and `basename` calls and is far faster inside loops.

head: Form
Result
Example with `f=/Users/sam/lab/backup.2026-10-07.tar.gz`
rows: value of `v`, or `word` if `v` is unset or empty
abort with `message` if `v` is unset or empty
`word` if `v` is set and non-empty, else nothing
zsh path modifiers: tail, head, root (no extension), extension
split into an array on commas

blocks.code:
$ f=/Users/sam/lab/backup.2026-10-07.tar.gz
$ echo "${f##*/}" "${f%/*}" "${f%%.*}" "${f:e}"
backup.2026-10-07.tar.gz /Users/sam/lab /Users/sam/lab/backup gz
$ csv="22,80,443"; ports=(${(s:,:)csv}); echo "${#ports} ports, last is $ports[-1]"
3 ports, last is 443
$ echo "${(j:+:)ports} = $(( ${(j:+:)ports} ))"
22+80+443 = 545
$ echo ${missing:-fallback} "[${(U)f:t}]"
fallback [BACKUP.2026-10-07.TAR.GZ]

blocks.text: Remember the pattern direction: `#` trims from the **front** (it is to the left of `$` on a US keyboard, and the number sign usually starts things), `%` trims from the **back**. Doubling the symbol means "longest match".

tokens.exp: start of an expansion
inner expansion: the file name of the path in f (zsh modifier :t, tail)
then drop the extension (modifier :r, root)
end; with f=/Users/sam/lab/report.csv the result is report

blocks.sum: Expand a variable with a default, a trim, a replacement, a case change or a split.

how.text: The shell evaluates `${...}` before running the command. The text after the name selects an operation. `:-`, `:=`, `:?` and `:+` handle unset or empty values; `#`, `##`, `%`, `%%` trim by glob pattern (not regex); `/` and `//` substitute. zsh adds **flags** in parentheses: `(U)` and `(L)` change case, `(s:x:)` splits on `x`, `(j:x:)` joins an array with `x`, `(f)` splits on newlines, `(k)` and `(v)` select keys or values of a map, `(o)` sorts.
Operations can be combined by nesting: `${${f##*/}%.gz}` first trims the folder, then the extension.

examples.desc: Default for a missing argument
File name without folder or extension
Rename every .txt to .bak using trimmed names
examples.code: for f in *.txt; do cp "$f" "${f%.txt}.bak"; done

examples.desc: Fail fast when a required value is missing

gotchas: Patterns after `#` and `%` are globs. `${f%.*}` removes a shell glob suffix, so a regex such as `[0-9]+` means nothing there.
`${v:-x}` treats an empty string like unset. `${v-x}` (no colon) substitutes only when `v` is unset.

blocks.text: Arithmetic
zsh does arithmetic natively, including **floating point**, which bash cannot. Two spellings cover it:

items.text: `(( expression ))` is a command: it evaluates and sets the exit status (0 when the result is non-zero). Use it for assignments (`(( n += 2 ))`), counters (`(( i++ ))`) and tests (`if (( n > 5 ))`).
`$(( expression ))` is an expansion: it is replaced by the result. Variables inside need no `$`.

blocks.text: If either operand has a decimal point the result is a float; two integers divide as integers, so `7 / 2` is 3. Write `7 / 2.0` when you want a fraction. Floats print with a trailing dot when whole (`4.`); use `printf '%.2f'` to control the format. `zsh/mathfunc` adds `sqrt`, `log`, `sin`, `abs`, `int` and more. For one-off floating-point work in a pipeline, `awk 'BEGIN {printf "%.2f\n", 7/2}'` and `bc -l` also work on every Mac.
Tests and branching
Every `if` runs a command and looks at its exit status: zero is true. The commands most often used for that are the test operators. zsh has two spellings, and you should know both.

head: Form
Where it comes from
Behaviour
rows: the original POSIX command (`[` is just a program name, and the final `]` is its last argument)
unquoted empty variables vanish, `-a` and `-o` are fragile, no pattern matching
no word splitting problems, `&&` `||` `( )` inside, glob patterns with `==`, regex with `=~`

blocks.text: Prefer `[[ ]]` in zsh scripts. Inside it, quoting variables is still good practice but not required for safety.

head: Test
True when
rows: string equal; with `[[ ]]` the right side is a glob pattern: `[[ $f == *.log ]]`
`s` matches the extended regex `re`; captures land in `$match[1]`, `$match[2]`, whole match in `$MATCH`

blocks.code:
$ [[ -f users.csv ]] && echo "users.csv exists"
users.csv exists
$ x=42; [[ $x == <-> ]] && echo "$x is an integer"
42 is an integer
$ line='alice,admin,10.0.0.5,22'
$ [[ $line =~ '^([a-z]+),([a-z]+),' ]] && echo "name=$match[1] role=$match[2]"
name=alice role=admin
$ [[ 5 -gt 3 && 2 -lt 1 ]]; echo "status $?"
status 1

blocks.text: `<->` is a zsh glob that matches any run of digits, a compact integer check. Note that `=~` uses ERE and that digit shortcuts such as `\d` are not available (see the flavour table in [the text toolkit](#text)).

blocks.sum: Evaluate a condition on files, strings, numbers, patterns or regexes, returning exit status 0 for true.

how.text: `[[` is a reserved word, so the shell parses the whole expression itself before any splitting or globbing happens. That is why an empty or space-containing variable cannot break it. Combine tests with `&&`, `||`, `!` and parentheses. With `==` and `!=` the right-hand side is a glob pattern unless quoted; with `=~` it is an extended regular expression and matches set `$MATCH` and the `$match` array.
Inside `[[ ]]` the operators `<` and `>` compare **strings**. For numbers write `-lt`/`-gt`, or use `(( ))`.

examples.desc: Is the argument an existing directory?
Match with a glob
Keep only the private 10.x lines of a list
examples.code: while read -r ip; do [[ $ip == 10.* ]] && echo $ip; done < ips.txt

gotchas: Quoting the right side of `==` turns the glob into a literal string: `[[ $f == "*.log" ]]` tests for a file literally named `*.log`.

blocks.name: test
blocks.sum: The POSIX test command, written `test expr` or `[ expr ]`, usable in any shell.

how.text: `[` is an ordinary command whose last argument must be `]`. Because it is a command, the shell expands its arguments first, so unquoted variables can vanish or split and change the meaning. In zsh `[ -n $x ]` with an empty `x` receives a single argument and wrongly reports true. Quote everything: `[ -n "$x" ]`. Use this form only when the script must also run under `sh`.

examples.desc: Numeric comparison, POSIX style
Test for a non-empty command result

gotchas: `[ $a = $b ]` breaks when `a` is empty (zsh drops the empty word and reports `condition expected`), and in bash or `sh` also when `a` contains spaces ("too many arguments"). `[[ $a = $b ]]` does neither.

blocks.sum: Evaluate an arithmetic expression; its status is 0 when the result is non-zero.

how.text: Inside the double parentheses, names are variables without `$`, numbers can be integer or floating point, and the operators follow C (add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, and a double-star operator for powers), plus comparisons, `&& || !`, bit operators and `++ --`. The command form sets `$?` so it works as a condition; the expansion form yields the text of the result.

examples.desc: Counter and condition
examples.code: (( i = 0 )); while (( i < 3 )); do echo "i=$i"; (( i++ )); done

examples.desc: Percentage with one decimal
Count matching lines and compare

gotchas: `(( x = 0 ))` returns status 1 because the result is 0. Under `setopt ERR_EXIT` that would abort the script, so use `x=0` for plain assignment.

blocks.name: if
blocks.sum: Run commands only when a condition command succeeds.
blocks.syntax: if cmd; then ...; [elif cmd; then ...;] [else ...;] fi

how.text: The condition is **any command**. Its exit status decides: 0 takes the `then` branch. That is why `if grep -q ERROR log` and `if ping -c 1 host >/dev/null` read naturally. `elif` chains further conditions and `else` handles the rest. `fi` closes the block.

examples.desc: Branch on a file test
examples.code: if [[ -f {{file}} ]]; then echo "found"; else echo "missing"; fi

examples.desc: Act on the result of a search
examples.code: if grep -q 'ERROR' notes.txt; then echo "has errors"; fi

blocks.name: case
blocks.sum: Compare a value against several glob patterns and run the commands of the first match.
blocks.syntax: case word in pattern1|pattern2) commands ;; pattern3) commands ;; *) default ;; esac

how.text: Each branch lists one or more glob patterns separated by `|`, a closing `)`, the commands and `;;`. The first matching branch runs and the rest are skipped. `*)` is the catch-all. `case` is cleaner than a chain of `elif` when you test one value, such as a subcommand name or a file extension.

examples.desc: Pick an action from a file extension
examples.code: case "{{file}}" in *.tar.gz|*.tgz) echo "tar";; *.zip) echo "zip";; *) echo "unknown";; esac

examples.desc: Classify every file in a folder
examples.code: for f in data/*; do case ${f:e} in log) echo "$f log";; txt) echo "$f text";; *) echo "$f other";; esac; done

gotchas: Each branch must end with `;;`. A missing one makes the shell read the next pattern as part of the commands and report a parse error.

blocks.text: Loops
zsh has several loop forms. They all share `do ... done` and the keywords `break` (leave the loop) and `continue` (skip to the next round).

head: Loop
Use it for
Example
rows: walking a list of words, files or an array
a fixed numeric range via brace expansion

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ for f in data/*.log; do echo $f $(wc -l < $f); done
data/delta.log 3
data/gamma.log 4
$ for h in $(cat hosts.txt); do echo ${#h} $h; done | sort -n | tail -2
13 wikipedia.org
14 cloudflare.com
$ total=0; for n in $(seq 1 5); do total=$((total + n)); done; echo $total
15

blocks.text: Reading a file line by line
`for line in $(cat file)` splits on **every** whitespace, so a line with spaces becomes several items. To process lines, use `while read`:

blocks.code:
$ while IFS=, read -r name role ip port; do [[ $role == dev ]] && echo "$name -> $ip:$port"; done < <(tail -n +2 users.csv)
bob -> 10.0.0.12:8080
carol -> 192.168.1.50:22
frank -> 172.16.0.9:443
judy -> 192.168.1.23:8000

blocks.text: Three details in that line: `IFS=,` sets the field separator for this one `read` so a CSV line splits into variables; `-r` stops `read` from treating backslashes as escapes; and `< <(...)` feeds the loop from a process substitution rather than a pipe. In zsh a pipe into `while` also works (the loop body runs in the current shell), but `< <(...)` or `< file` is portable and avoids a surprise in bash.

blocks.name: for
blocks.sum: Repeat commands once for each word in a list, each element of an array, or each value of a counter.
blocks.syntax: for name in word ...; do commands; done      for ((init; cond; step)); do commands; done

how.text: The list is expanded **before** the loop starts: globs, braces and command substitutions turn into words, and `name` takes each in turn. Quote the pieces you create yourself, and use a glob rather than `$(ls)`, which breaks on spaces. In zsh an unmatched glob is an error, so add the `(N)` qualifier (`for f in *.log(N)`) when an empty list is acceptable.

examples.desc: Back up every .txt file
examples.code: for f in *.txt; do cp "$f" "$f.bak"; done

examples.desc: Print the line count of each log, largest first
examples.code: for f in data/*.log; do echo "$(wc -l < $f) $f"; done | sort -rn

blocks.name: while
blocks.sum: Run commands as long as a condition command succeeds; `until` runs until it succeeds.
blocks.syntax: while cmd; do commands; done      until cmd; do commands; done

how.text: The condition is run before each round, and any command qualifies: a test, `grep -q`, `ping`, or `read`, which succeeds until the input ends. `while read -r line; do ...; done < file` is the standard line-by-line loop. For waiting, `until ping -c 1 -t 2 host >/dev/null; do sleep 2; done` blocks until a machine comes back.

examples.desc: Wait for a host to answer
examples.code: until ping -c 1 -t 2 {{host}} > /dev/null; do echo "waiting..."; sleep 2; done; echo "up"

examples.desc: Number the lines that contain ERROR
examples.code: n=0; while read -r l; do (( n++ )); [[ $l == *ERROR* ]] && echo "$n: $l"; done < notes.txt

gotchas: `while true; do ...; done` loops forever; stop it with [[Ctrl+C]]. Always put a `sleep` inside a loop that polls, or it will spin at 100 percent CPU.

blocks.name: repeat
blocks.sum: Run a command a fixed number of times (a zsh keyword).
blocks.syntax: repeat count command      repeat count; do commands; done

how.text: `repeat 3 echo hi` prints three lines. It is shorter than a counting `for` when you do not need the counter, and handy for timing or load tests. It exists in zsh but not in bash, so avoid it in scripts you share.

examples.desc: Ping a host five times with a pause

blocks.name: select
blocks.sum: Print a numbered menu from a list and run commands with the chosen item in a variable.
blocks.syntax: select name in word ...; do commands; done

how.text: `select` prints the words numbered on stderr, shows the prompt in `$PS3` and reads a number. The chosen word goes into `name`, the raw input into `$REPLY`, and the body runs. The loop repeats until `break`, so give the user a "quit" entry. An invalid number leaves `name` empty, which a `*)` branch can catch.

examples.desc: A tiny network menu
examples.code: PS3="check> "; select act in gateway dns quit; do case $act in gateway) route -n get default | grep gateway;; dns) scutil --dns | grep -m1 nameserver;; quit) break;; *) echo "pick 1-3";; esac; done

gotchas: Reading from a pipe works but the menu is no use unattended. Use `select` only in interactive scripts.

blocks.name: read
blocks.sum: Read one line from stdin, split it into variables, with options for prompts, silence and timeouts.

how.text: `read` takes a line from stdin, splits it on `$IFS` and assigns the pieces to the names; the last name gets the remainder. `-r` keeps backslashes literal and should be used almost always. `-s` does not echo what is typed (passwords), `-t N` gives up after N seconds with a non-zero status, `-k N` reads N characters without waiting for Enter. The loop `while read -r line; do ...; done < file` ends when `read` hits end of input.

zsh's prompt syntax is `read "answer?Continue? "`, a question mark inside the first name. Careful: the Bash form `read -p "prompt" var` means something else in zsh (`-p` reads from a coprocess) and fails.

examples.desc: Ask a question with a default
Split a line into fields
examples.code: IFS=: read -r user x uid rest <<< "root:x:0:0:System"; echo "$user $uid"

examples.desc: Process a CSV, skipping the header
examples.code: tail -n +2 users.csv | while IFS=, read -r name role ip port; do echo "$name:$ip"; done

gotchas: `read` strips leading and trailing whitespace from the line unless you set `IFS=` (empty): `while IFS= read -r line` preserves it.

tokens.exp: keyword: compare one word against patterns
the value being tested: the file's extension
start of the branch list
pattern with a closing parenthesis; several patterns are joined with |
commands to run when it matches
end of this branch
a catch-all pattern placed last
case spelled backwards ends the block

blocks.text: Functions

A **function** names a block of commands so you can call it like any other command. It receives its own positional parameters (`$1`, `$#`, `"$@"`), has an exit status, and can print data to stdout for the caller to capture.

blocks.code:
$ greet() { local who=${1:-world}; print "hello, $who"; }
$ greet; greet Ada
hello, world
hello, Ada
$ who=outer; h() { local who=inner; echo $who; }; h; echo $who
inner
outer
$ f() { local n=$1; if (( n < 2 )); then echo $n; return; fi; echo $(( n * 2 )); }
$ r=$(f 21); echo "captured: $r"
captured: 42
$ g() { return 3; }; g; echo "status: $?"
status: 3

blocks.text: There are two separate ways a function reports back, and mixing them up is a common mistake:

items.text: **Exit status** (`return N`, 0 to 255): success or failure, tested with `if f; then`. It is not for data.
**Output** (anything printed to stdout): the data, captured with `result=$(f args)`. Send diagnostic messages to stderr (`print -u2 "message"`) so they do not pollute the captured result.

blocks.text: Variables inside functions are global unless declared `local` (or `typeset`). Forgetting `local` is how loop counters named `i` collide across functions. Define functions before the code that calls them.

blocks.name: function
blocks.sum: Define a named, reusable block of commands with its own arguments and local variables.

how.text: The shell stores the body and runs it when you use the name as a command. Arguments become `$1`, `$2`, `$#` and `"$@"` inside, and the script's own arguments are hidden until the function returns. A function can call itself, call other functions and use `return`. `local` and `typeset` create variables that disappear on return. In an interactive shell, `functions name` prints a definition and `unfunction name` removes it.

examples.desc: A function with a default argument and a return status
A helper that returns data through stdout
examples.code: top_ip() { awk '{print $1}' "$1" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1 | awk '{print $2}'; }; echo "busiest: $(top_ip access.log)"

gotchas: A function's last command decides its exit status. Add an explicit `return 0` or `return 1` when that matters.
Unlike scripts, functions are not run in a child process, so `cd` inside one changes the caller's directory.

blocks.name: local
blocks.sum: Declare a variable that exists only inside the current function.

how.text: `local` is the zsh/bash spelling of `typeset` inside a function. The variable shadows any global of the same name and is discarded when the function returns, which keeps counters and temporary strings from leaking. A common pattern is `local line count=0`. Write `local out; out=$(cmd)` rather than `local out=$(cmd)` if you need the exit status of `cmd`: with the combined form `$?` is the status of `local`, which succeeds.

examples.desc: A function with private variables
examples.code: total() { local sum=0 n; for n in "$@"; do (( sum += n )); done; echo $sum; }; total 4 5 6

blocks.name: return
blocks.sum: Leave a function immediately, giving the exit status the caller will see in $?.

how.text: With no argument `return` uses the status of the last command. Statuses are integers from 0 to 255; 0 means success. To send text or numbers larger than 255 to the caller, print them and capture with `$(...)`. Outside a function or sourced script, use `exit` instead.

examples.desc: Fail a check with a status
Use the status in a pipeline's condition
examples.code: need_file users.csv && cut -d, -f1 users.csv | tail -n +2 | head -3

blocks.name: shift
blocks.sum: Discard the first positional parameter (or the first N) and renumber the rest.

how.text: After `shift`, `$2` becomes `$1`, `$#` decreases by one and `"$@"` has one fewer item. It is how scripts walk through arguments and how they remove options so that the remaining words are the file names.

examples.desc: Take the first argument as a command word and pass on the rest
Process every remaining argument

gotchas: `shift` with nothing left is an error in some shells. Test `(( $# ))` first.

blocks.text: Options: getopts and zparseopts

Real tools take options (`-q`, `-n 5`, `-d example.com`). Two mechanisms parse them. `getopts` is a builtin present in every POSIX shell; `zparseopts` is zsh's more flexible option parser (long options, optional values, any position).

blocks.code:
$ ./opts.zsh -n 3 -v a.txt b.txt
count=3 verbose=1 files: a.txt b.txt
$ ./opts.zsh -n
option -n needs a value
$ ./opts.zsh -z
unknown option -z

blocks.text: In the option string, a letter followed by `:` takes a value (`n:`), and the leading `:` turns on silent mode, in which you handle errors yourself: a missing value sets `opt` to `:`, an unknown option sets it to `?`. `OPTARG` holds the value and `OPTIND` the index of the next argument, so `shift $((OPTIND - 1))` leaves only the non-option arguments.

blocks.name: getopts
blocks.sum: Parse short options (-v, -n 5) one at a time inside a while loop.
blocks.syntax: while getopts "optstring" var; do case $var in ...; esac; done

how.text: Each call to `getopts` examines the next argument. It stores the option letter in `var`, any value in `$OPTARG` and advances `$OPTIND`. It stops at the first argument that does not start with `-`, or at `--`. It supports only single-letter options; for `--verbose` style use `zparseopts`.

examples.desc: Boolean flag and option with a value
examples.code: while getopts "qd:" o; do case $o in q) quiet=1;; d) domain=$OPTARG;; esac; done; shift $((OPTIND-1))

gotchas: Options after the first non-option word are not seen: `script file -v` leaves `-v` as an ordinary argument. Put options first or use `zparseopts -E`.

blocks.name: zparseopts
blocks.sum: zsh's option parser: pull options out of $@ into variables or arrays, in any position.

how.text: Each `spec` names an option: `v` is a flag, `n:` takes a required value, `n::` an optional one, `-verbose` a long option, and `v=verbose` stores the result in the array `verbose`. `-D` deletes the parsed options from `$@`, `-E` keeps scanning past arguments that are not options so flags may appear anywhere, and `-F` aborts on an unknown option. After parsing, `(( $#verbose ))` is true if `-v` was given and `$count[-1]` is the value of `-n 5`.

examples.desc: Flags anywhere on the line
examples.code:
zparseopts -D -E -F -- v=verbose n:=count || exit 2
echo "verbose=($verbose) count=($count) rest=($@)"

gotchas: The results are arrays holding the option **and** its value (`-n 5`), so use `$count[-1]` for the value, not `$count`.

blocks.text: Failing safely

By default a script keeps going after errors: a failed `cd` is followed by an `rm` in the wrong folder, or a typo in a variable name expands to nothing. Three options turn those silent failures into stops:

head: Option
Effect
Why
rows: exit when a simple command fails
stops the cascade after the first error
using an unset variable is an error
a pipeline fails if any stage fails

blocks.text: Put `setopt ERR_EXIT NO_UNSET PIPE_FAIL` near the top of scripts that change things. `ERR_EXIT` ignores failures in places where a failure is expected: the condition of an `if`, anything before `&&` or `||`, and negated commands. Add `|| true` after a command whose failure you accept (`grep -q x file || true`).

blocks.title: Variables inside rm are a loaded gun

blocks.text: `rm -rf "$BUILD_DIR"/*` expands to `rm -rf /*` if `BUILD_DIR` is empty, and macOS will start removing whatever your user may delete. `NO_UNSET` catches a missing variable, and `${BUILD_DIR:?}` aborts on an empty one. Better: `echo` or `ls` the expanded command first, and try destructive scripts on a copy in `~/lab`.
trap: clean up whatever happens

`trap 'commands' SIGNAL...` registers commands the shell runs when it receives a signal or leaves. The pseudo-signal `EXIT` fires whenever the script exits, normally, through `exit` or through `ERR_EXIT`, which makes it the right place to delete temporary files. In zsh it does **not** fire when an untrapped signal such as Ctrl-C kills the script, so add `trap 'exit 130' INT TERM` to turn those signals into an ordinary exit.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
setopt ERR_EXIT NO_UNSET PIPE_FAIL
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"; print "cleanup done"' EXIT
print "working in $tmp"
cp /nonexistent "$tmp/"
print "never printed"

$ ./safe.zsh
working in /var/folders/zz/k3x9/T/tmp.p2QeW8yL
cp: /nonexistent: No such file or directory
cleanup done

blocks.text: The `cp` failed, `ERR_EXIT` ended the script before the last line, and the `EXIT` trap still removed the temporary folder.

blocks.name: trap
blocks.sum: Run commands when the shell receives a signal or exits.

how.text: The commands string is stored and executed when one of the listed signals arrives (`INT` is Ctrl-C, `TERM` is the default `kill`, `HUP` is a closed terminal) or, for `EXIT`, when the shell exits (in zsh, not when an untrapped signal kills it). `trap - SIGNAL` restores default handling. Signals `KILL` and `STOP` cannot be caught. Use single quotes so that variables are expanded when the trap runs, not when it is set.

examples.desc: Remove a temp file on exit or interrupt
Stop a long-running loop cleanly on Ctrl-C and print the total
examples.code: n=0; trap 'echo "processed $n"; exit 130' INT; while read -r l; do (( n++ )); sleep 0.01; done < access.log

gotchas: A trap on `INT` that does not call `exit` makes Ctrl-C resume the script instead of stopping it.

blocks.name: mktemp
blocks.sum: Create a uniquely named temporary file or directory and print its path.

how.text: `mktemp` creates the file atomically with permissions only you can use, so two runs never collide and another user cannot guess the name, unlike `/tmp/myscript.$$`. With `-d` it makes a directory. With no template, the macOS version places the item under `$TMPDIR` (a per-user folder under `/var/folders`).

flags.d: Create a directory instead of a file.
Use the temporary folder and the given prefix.

examples.desc: Scratch directory removed on exit
Sort a file safely and replace it

blocks.text: Debugging scripts
When a script misbehaves, work from cheap checks to detailed ones:

items.text: **Syntax check without running**: `zsh -n script.zsh`. It catches unclosed quotes, missing `fi`/`done` and similar errors, and prints nothing when the syntax is fine.

**Trace execution**: `zsh -x script.zsh` (or `setopt xtrace` inside the script) prints every command after expansion with a `+` prefix, so you see the real values. Change the prefix with `PS4='+%N:%i> '` to show the file name and line number.
**Skip your startup files while tracing** with `zsh -f -x script.zsh`, so that only the script is traced.
**Print the suspects**: `print -u2 "DEBUG n=$n"` writes to stderr and stays out of pipes and captured output.
**Shrink it**: copy the failing part into a new file with fixed inputs until it still fails and cannot get smaller.

blocks.code:
$ PS4='+%N:%i> ' zsh -f -x args.zsh a b 2>&1 | head -6
+args.zsh:2> echo 'script: args.zsh'
script: args.zsh
+args.zsh:3> echo 'count:  2'
count:  2
+args.zsh:4> echo 'first:  a'
first:  a

blocks.text: `brew install shellcheck` gives you an excellent linter for `sh`, `bash`, `dash` and `ksh` scripts, but it cannot parse zsh-only syntax such as `${(U)v}`, `repeat` or glob qualifiers, and will report false errors. Use it for POSIX scripts, and rely on `zsh -n`, `zsh -x` and careful reading for zsh.
Common mistakes

head: Symptom
Cause
Fix
rows: `bad interpreter` or `zsh: no such file` on line 1
wrong shebang path or Windows line endings
a loop variable keeps an old value
filenames with spaces split in the middle
script works in Terminal, fails in cron
absolute paths, set `PATH` at the top

blocks.text: Running scripts on a schedule
Most useful scripts run without you: a check every five minutes, a backup every night. macOS offers two schedulers.
**cron** is the classic. `crontab -e` edits your table, `crontab -l` lists it. Each line has five time fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) and a command:

blocks.code:
*/5 * * * *   /Users/{{user}}/bin/netcheck.zsh -q >> /tmp/netcheck.log 2>&1
30 2 * * *    /Users/{{user}}/bin/backup.zsh /Users/{{user}}/lab /Users/{{user}}/backups 7

blocks.text: Cron runs commands with an almost empty environment: `PATH` is just `/usr/bin:/bin`, there is no `.zshrc`, and the working directory is your home. Use absolute paths and redirect output to a file. On recent macOS versions cron also needs **Full Disk Access** (System Settings, Privacy & Security) before it can touch protected folders such as Documents and Desktop, which is one reason Apple prefers launchd.
**launchd** is the macOS-native way. A job is a property-list file in `~/Library/LaunchAgents/` that launchd loads for your login session:

blocks.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>
  <string>local.netcheck</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/Users/{{user}}/bin/netcheck.zsh</string>
    <string>-q</string>
  </array>
  <key>StartInterval</key>
  <integer>300</integer>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key>
  <string>/tmp/netcheck.out</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
  <string>/tmp/netcheck.err</string>
</dict>
</plist>

blocks.text: Property lists do not expand `~` or `$HOME`, so paths must be absolute. Load, inspect and unload with the modern `launchctl` verbs:

blocks.code:
plutil -lint ~/Library/LaunchAgents/local.netcheck.plist
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/local.netcheck.plist
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/local.netcheck | head -20
launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/local.netcheck
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/local.netcheck

blocks.name: crontab
blocks.sum: Edit, list or remove your table of scheduled jobs.

how.text: The five fields are `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`; `*` means every value, `*/5` every fifth, `1-5` a range, `1,15` a list. The job runs in a minimal environment with `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin`, so give full paths and send output to a file or it is mailed to the local mailbox and lost. `-r` deletes the whole table without asking.

examples.desc: Run a script every five minutes and keep its log
Show only the active jobs, not the comments

gotchas: `crontab -r` is one letter from `-e`. Run `crontab -l > ~/crontab.bak` before editing.

blocks.name: launchctl
blocks.sum: Load, start, inspect and unload launchd jobs, the macOS scheduler for scripts and daemons.
blocks.syntax: launchctl bootstrap gui/UID plist      launchctl bootout gui/UID/label      launchctl print gui/UID/label

how.text: launchd reads job definitions from property lists and starts them on a schedule (`StartInterval` seconds, `StartCalendarInterval` clock times), at login (`RunAtLoad`) or on demand. Jobs for your own user live in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, use the domain `gui/$(id -u)`, and need no sudo. `bootstrap` loads a plist, `bootout` unloads a job by its label, `kickstart -k` restarts it now and `print` shows state and last exit status. The older `load` and `unload` verbs still work but are deprecated.

examples.desc: Install and start a user job
See why a job failed
List your loaded jobs that you wrote (label prefix local.)

gotchas: `bootstrap` errors with "Input/output error" when the job is already loaded or the plist has the wrong owner or syntax. `bootout` first, run `plutil -lint`, then bootstrap again.

blocks.text: Dates, delays and timing

blocks.name: date
blocks.sum: Print or compute dates and times, with the BSD options macOS provides.

how.text: `date +FORMAT` prints the current time using `strftime` codes: `%F` is `2026-10-07`, `%T` is `14:05:09`, `%s` is the Unix timestamp in seconds, `%a %b %e` give weekday and month names. **BSD date** differs from GNU date: `-v` adjusts the time (`-v-1d` is yesterday, `-v+2H` is two hours ahead, `-v1d` sets the day of month to 1), and `-j -f FORMAT STRING` parses a date string without setting the clock. GNU's `date -d "yesterday"` does not exist on macOS.

flags.d: Adjust a field: `-v-7d`, `-v+1m`, `-v0H`; may be repeated.
Parse a given date string by format, without setting the system clock.

examples.desc: Timestamp for a file name
Yesterday's date
Convert a date to a Unix timestamp
Log lines with a timestamp prefix
examples.code: ping -c 3 {{host}} | while read -r l; do echo "$(date +%T) $l"; done

gotchas: `date -d '...'` and `date --date` are GNU only. On macOS use `-v` and `-j -f`.

blocks.name: sleep
blocks.sum: Pause for a number of seconds, fractions allowed on macOS.

how.text: The shell waits without using CPU. macOS accepts decimals (`sleep 0.5`), which is useful in polling loops. Put a `sleep` in any loop that checks something over and over.

examples.desc: Poll every two seconds

blocks.name: time
blocks.sum: Report how long a command took (the zsh keyword prints user, system and wall-clock time).

how.text: In zsh, `time` is a reserved word that can time an entire pipeline and prints a line such as `0.02s user 0.01s system 91% cpu 0.031 total`. The last number is wall-clock time. Customize the format with the `TIMEFMT` variable. The external `/usr/bin/time -l` also reports peak memory.

examples.desc: Time a pipeline
examples.code: time (awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3)

blocks.name: watch
blocks.sum: Run a command repeatedly and refresh the output on screen (needs brew install watch).

how.text: macOS does not ship `watch`. After `brew install watch`, `watch -n 2 'netstat -an | grep -c ESTABLISHED'` re-runs a command every two seconds and redraws, with `-d` highlighting what changed. Without installing anything you can write the same thing as `while true; do clear; command; sleep 2; done`.

examples.desc: Watch the established connections
Poor man's watch with no install
examples.code: while true; do clear; date; netstat -an | grep -c ESTABLISHED; sleep 2; done

blocks.text: Project: netcheck.zsh

`netcheck.zsh` answers "is my network healthy?" in two seconds. It checks, in order: the default route and interface, your IP address, the gateway, a DNS lookup, an internet host, and an HTTP request. Each check prints a coloured `OK` or `FAIL` line, and the script's **exit status is the number of failures**, so other scripts and launchd can use it. The commands it relies on are the read-only ones you met in [Pipes](#pipes); [See your own network](#net-local) explains their output in detail.
Step 1: The skeleton, options and output helpers
Create `~/bin/netcheck.zsh` (`nano ~/bin/netcheck.zsh`, or a PyCharm scratch file). Start with settings, option parsing and the two helpers every check will call:

The colour variables are empty when output is not a terminal (`-t 1`), so redirecting to a file produces clean text. Notice the quotes around `"$c_ok"`: an empty unquoted variable would disappear from the `printf` arguments and shift every other one.
Step 2: Interface, address and gateway
Add the checks that read the routing table. `route -n get default` prints `interface:` and `gateway:` lines; `ipconfig getifaddr` prints the interface's IPv4 address.

blocks.code:
check_route() {
  iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
  gw=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}')
  if [[ -z $iface ]]; then
    fail "default route" "none: no usable network"
    return 1
  fi
  pass "default route" "via $iface"
  myip=$(ipconfig getifaddr $iface 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ -z $myip ]]; then
    fail "IP address" "$iface has no IPv4 address"
  elif [[ $myip == 169.254.* ]]; then
    fail "IP address" "$myip is link-local: DHCP failed"
  else
    pass "IP address" "$myip"
  fi
}

check_gateway() {
  [[ -n $gw ]] || { pass "gateway" "none (point-to-point link)"; return }
  local avg
  avg=$(ping -c 3 -t 5 $gw 2>/dev/null | awk -F/ '/round-trip/ {printf "%.1f", $5}')
  if [[ -n $avg ]]; then
    pass "gateway $gw" "${avg} ms average"
  else
    fail "gateway $gw" "no reply to ping"
  fi
}

blocks.text: The ping summary line is `round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 1.1/2.2/3.3/0.5 ms`. Splitting on `/` makes the average field 5. An address starting `169.254.` means DHCP never answered and macOS assigned itself a link-local address, which deserves its own message because it points straight at the cause.
Step 3: DNS and the internet

DNS gets its own timing, using zsh's `$EPOCHREALTIME`. The internet check pings a public address by number, so a failure there with a working gateway but a *working* DNS check tells you the problem is upstream, while DNS failing alone points at the resolver.

blocks.code:
check_dns() {
  local t0=$EPOCHREALTIME answer ms
  answer=$(dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 $domain A 2>/dev/null |
           grep -E '^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$' | head -1)
  ms=$(( (EPOCHREALTIME - t0) * 1000 ))
  if [[ -n $answer ]]; then
    pass "DNS $domain" "$answer ($(printf '%.0f' $ms) ms)"
  else
    fail "DNS $domain" "no A record returned"
  fi
}

check_internet() {
  local avg
  avg=$(ping -c 2 -t 4 1.1.1.1 2>/dev/null | awk -F/ '/round-trip/ {printf "%.1f", $5}')
  if [[ -n $avg ]]; then
    pass "internet 1.1.1.1" "${avg} ms average"
  else
    fail "internet 1.1.1.1" "no reply (try: ping -c 2 8.8.8.8)"
  fi
}

blocks.text: `dig +short` prints CNAME targets as well as addresses, and prints nothing useful on failure, so the `grep -E` keeps only a line that looks like an IPv4 address. The options `+time=2 +tries=1` bound the wait to about two seconds instead of the default several attempts.
Step 4: HTTP, the summary and the exit code
The HTTP check uses `curl -w` to print the status code and total time, and treats any 2xx or 3xx as success. Then the main section runs the checks and turns the failure count into the exit status.

blocks.code:
check_http() {
  local out code secs
  out=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -m 6 -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}' $url 2>/dev/null)
  code=${out%% *}
  secs=${out##* }
  if [[ $code == [23]* ]]; then
    pass "HTTP $url" "$code in ${secs}s"
  else
    fail "HTTP $url" "status ${code:-none}"
  fi
}

check_route && check_gateway
check_dns
check_internet
check_http

if (( fails )); then
  print -u2 "netcheck: $fails check(s) failed"
else
  (( quiet )) || print "all checks passed"
fi
exit $(( fails > 255 ? 255 : fails ))

blocks.text: `check_route && check_gateway` skips the gateway test when there is no route, since it would only add noise. Make the script executable and run it:

blocks.code:
chmod +x ~/bin/netcheck.zsh
netcheck.zsh
netcheck.zsh -q; echo "failures: $?"
netcheck.zsh -d example.org -u https://example.org

$ netcheck.zsh
[ OK ] default route            via en0
[ OK ] IP address               192.168.1.23
[ OK ] gateway 192.168.1.1      2.4 ms average
[ OK ] DNS example.com          93.184.216.34 (31 ms)
[ OK ] internet 1.1.1.1         11.8 ms average
[ OK ] HTTP https://example.com 200 in 0.142s
all checks passed
$ netcheck.zsh -q; echo "failures: $?"
failures: 0

blocks.text: Turn Wi-Fi off from the menu bar and run `netcheck.zsh` again. You should see the first check fail and the rest report why. Turn it back on and try `netcheck.zsh -d does-not-exist.invalid`: only the DNS line should fail, and `echo $?` should print 1. A tool you have watched fail correctly is a tool you can trust.

Add a `-w` option that waits and repeats every N seconds. Add a check for your DNS server from `scutil --dns`. Write the output to `~/netcheck.log` with a timestamp when a check fails. Schedule `netcheck.zsh -q` every five minutes with launchd and look at the log tomorrow. [Troubleshooting](#troubleshoot) extends this script into `netdoctor.zsh`.

A backup script makes a dated archive of a folder and deletes the oldest archives beyond a limit. It exercises arguments with defaults, validation, `trap` for cleanup of partial files and zsh's glob qualifiers for rotation.
Step 1: Archive with a timestamp

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# backup.zsh - tar a folder into a dated archive and keep only the newest N
# Usage: backup.zsh SOURCE_DIR [DEST_DIR] [KEEP]
setopt ERR_EXIT NO_UNSET PIPE_FAIL

src=${1:?usage: backup.zsh SOURCE_DIR [DEST_DIR] [KEEP]}
dest=${2:-$HOME/backups}
keep=${3:-5}

[[ -d $src ]] || { print -u2 "backup: $src is not a directory"; exit 1 }
[[ $keep == <-> && $keep -ge 1 ]] || { print -u2 "backup: KEEP must be a positive integer"; exit 1 }
mkdir -p $dest

name=${src:A:t}                                  # absolute path, then last component
stamp=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
archive=$dest/$name-$stamp.tgz

trap 'rm -f $archive; print -u2 "backup: interrupted, removed partial archive"' INT TERM
tar -czf $archive -C ${src:A:h} $name
trap - INT TERM
print "created $archive ($(du -h $archive | awk '{print $1}'))"

# rotation: list this folder's archives newest first, delete everything after the first $keep
old=($dest/$name-*.tgz(N.om[$((keep + 1)),-1]))
if (( $#old )); then
  rm -- $old
  print "removed ${#old} old archive(s)"
fi

blocks.text: `${src:A:t}` first makes the path absolute (`:A`) then takes the last component (`:t`), so `backup.zsh .` still names the archive after the real folder. `tar -C dir name` changes into `dir` first, so the archive holds `name/...` rather than absolute paths.
Step 2: Understand the rotation line

`$dest/$name-*.tgz(N.om[4,-1])` is a glob with qualifiers in parentheses. `N` returns an empty list instead of an error when nothing matches, `.` keeps regular files only, `om` sorts by modification time, newest first, and `[4,-1]` selects the fourth element through the last. With `keep=3`, that is everything older than the three newest archives. Test it safely with `print -l` before you trust it with `rm`:

blocks.code:
mkdir -p ~/lab/bk-test && cd ~/lab/bk-test
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do touch -t 20260101010$i f$i.tgz; done
print -l *.tgz(N.om[4,-1])

blocks.text: Step 3: Run it

blocks.code:
mkdir -p ~/lab/demo-src && echo hello > ~/lab/demo-src/a.txt
chmod +x backup.zsh
for i in 1 2 3 4; do ./backup.zsh ~/lab/demo-src ~/lab/backups 2; sleep 1; done
ls ~/lab/backups

blocks.text: After the loop `ls` shows only the two newest archives. Run `./backup.zsh /nonexistent` and `./backup.zsh ~/lab/demo-src ~/lab/backups abc` to see both validations fail with status 1.
Add an `-x pattern` option that excludes files (`tar --exclude`). Verify each archive with `tar -tzf` and delete it if listing fails. Log every run to `~/backups/backup.log` with `tee -a`.
Practice

blocks.title: Count lines per log

task.text: In `~/lab`, print each `.log` file in `data/` followed by its line count on one line (for example `data/delta.log 3`). Use a `for` loop and command substitution.

hints: The glob `data/*.log` expands to the files.
`wc -l < "$f"` prints a number without the name.
blocks.solution: for f in data/*.log; do echo "$f $(wc -l < "$f" | tr -d ' ')"; done

why.text: The glob supplies the words, `$( )` captures a result per file. `tr -d ' '` removes the padding macOS puts in front of `wc` numbers.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose: the space in the assignment

task.text: Run `count = 5` and read the error. Then fix the assignment and print the value. Explain why the first form failed.

hints: Look at what the shell tried to execute.

why.text: With spaces, the shell looks for a **command** named `count` and passes `=` and `5` as arguments, so you get "command not found". An assignment is a single word with no spaces around `=`.

blocks.title: Argument parser

task.text: Write `greet.zsh` that accepts `-n NAME` (default `world`), `-u` (upper-case the greeting) and `-h` (usage, exit 0). An unknown option prints usage to stderr and exits 2. Test all four paths and check the exit codes with `echo $?`.

why.text: `getopts` loops over options; `shift` is not needed because the script takes no file arguments. The script name is saved in `prog` first because inside a function `$0` is the function's name. Sending usage to stderr with status 2 follows the convention that 2 means misuse.

blocks.title: A menu with select

task.text: Write `menu.zsh` that shows a `select` menu with the entries `time`, `whoami`, `uptime` and `quit`. Choosing an entry runs the command, `quit` ends the script, and any other number prints `invalid choice`.

hints: Set `PS3` for the prompt, and put a `case` inside the `select` body.

why.text: `select` stores the chosen word in `item`; an invalid number leaves it empty, which the `*)` branch handles. `break` is the only way out of the loop.

blocks.title: Log rotator

task.text: Write `rotate.zsh LOGFILE KEEP`. It renames `LOGFILE` to `LOGFILE.1`, shifting existing `LOGFILE.1` to `.2` and so on, and deletes anything beyond `KEEP` generations. Create an empty `LOGFILE` afterwards. Test it on a copy of `access.log`.

hints: Work from the oldest to the newest so you never overwrite a file you still need: a `for` loop counting down.

why.text: Shifting from the highest number down means each `mv` target is already free. `: > file` is the idiom for creating or truncating a file with no output.

blocks.title: Status code reporter

task.text: Write `codes.zsh LOGFILE` that reads the log with `while read`, counts each status code (field 9) in an associative array, and prints `code count` lines sorted by code. It must exit 1 with a usage message when no file is given.

hints: Split each line into an array with `parts=(${=line})` and take `$parts[9]`.
blocks.solution:
#!/bin/zsh
log=${1:?usage: codes.zsh LOGFILE}
typeset -A seen
while read -r line; do
  parts=(${=line})
  (( seen[$parts[9]]++ ))
done < $log
for k in ${(ko)seen}; do print "$k $seen[$k]"; done

why.text: `${=line}` splits on whitespace, 1-indexed arrays make field 9 `$parts[9]`, and `${(ko)seen}` iterates keys in sorted order. The same job in `awk` is shorter, but writing it in the shell teaches arrays, loops and expansion.

blocks.title: Safe temp work

task.text: Write a script that creates a temporary directory, copies `~/lab/hosts.txt` into it, sorts the copy in place and prints the first line, and always removes the directory when it ends, even when you interrupt it with Ctrl-C. Prove the cleanup by adding `sleep 30` and pressing Ctrl-C.

blocks.solution:
#!/bin/zsh
setopt ERR_EXIT NO_UNSET PIPE_FAIL
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"; print "removed $tmp"' EXIT
trap 'exit 130' INT TERM
cp ~/lab/hosts.txt "$tmp/"
sort -o "$tmp/hosts.txt" "$tmp/hosts.txt"
head -1 "$tmp/hosts.txt"
sleep 30

why.text: The `EXIT` trap runs whenever the script exits. In zsh an untrapped Ctrl-C kills the script without running it, so the `INT TERM` trap turns the signal into an ordinary `exit 130`, and the cleanup runs. `sort -o` is the safe in-place sort because it writes after reading.

questions.q: What does `./script.zsh` need that `zsh script.zsh` does not?

options.text: The execute permission bit and a shebang line

questions.why: Running `./script.zsh` asks the kernel to execute the file, which needs `chmod +x` and a shebang naming the interpreter. `zsh script.zsh` names the interpreter itself and only needs read access.

questions.q: In zsh, what is `${arr[1]}` for `arr=(x y z)`?
questions.why: zsh arrays are 1-indexed, unlike bash. `$arr[-1]` is the last element.

options.text: Removes everything up to the first dot
Removes the shortest suffix matching `.*`, leaving `report.final`
Replaces the dot with a percent sign

questions.why: A single `%` removes the shortest matching suffix, so only `.csv` goes. `%%` would remove the longest, `.final.csv`.

questions.q: A function prints a number with `echo` and also calls `return 5`. How does the caller get each?

options.text: The number from `$?`, the status from `$(f)`
The number from `$(f)`, the status from `$?`

questions.why: Output is data captured with command substitution. The `return` value is an exit status in `$?`, limited to 0 to 255.

questions.q: Which `setopt` line turns a failed stage in `a | b | c` into a failed pipeline?
questions.why: `PIPE_FAIL` (case and underscores are ignored by `setopt`, so `pipefail` works too) makes the pipeline's status the rightmost non-zero status of any stage.

questions.q: Why does `printf '%s|%s\n' $empty x` print `x|` rather than `|x` in zsh?

options.text: An unquoted empty variable is removed, so `x` becomes the first argument

questions.why: zsh does not word-split variables but it still removes an unquoted empty expansion. Writing `"$empty"` keeps an empty argument in place.

blocks.text: Try it in the practice terminal
The simulator supports single-line `for` loops, `if` blocks, `$(( ))` arithmetic and command substitution, which is enough for the three missions. Multi-line scripts need your real Terminal.

terms.def: First line of a script, `#!` plus an interpreter path, that tells the kernel how to run the file
Number from 0 to 255 a command leaves behind; 0 means success
An argument passed to a script or function, available as $1, $2 and so on
A child copy of the shell, created by `( )`, `$( )` or a pipeline, whose changes do not affect the parent
The ${...} syntax that supplies defaults, trims, replaces and transforms variable values
zsh suffix in parentheses after a glob that filters matches by type, age, size or order
A command registered to run when the shell receives a signal or exits
The macOS service manager that starts and schedules jobs from property-list files
The traditional Unix scheduler driven by a five-field crontab table
Shell option that prints each command after expansion, used to debug scripts
A variable limited to the function that declares it
A map from string keys to values, declared in zsh with typeset -A
